III · Arithmetic

VI. Optimized binary gcd iteration

IonQ changes how the current gcd remainders are stored, while still recording each decision. This turns controlled subtraction into a cheaper choice between addition and subtraction.

6 min core readingp. 12Coverage & audit

Why point addition needs a gcd computation

Suppose we need to divide 4 by 5 modulo 7. We are looking for a number that gives remainder 4 when multiplied by 5. The answer is 5, because 25 leaves remainder 4. Point addition needs this same operation on 256-bit numbers: the numerator and denominator are differences between two points' coordinates.

The two points are the accumulator (x1,y1)(x_1,y_1)(x1​,y1​) and a selected table point (x2,y2)(x_2,y_2)(x2​,y2​). Subtract their coordinates to obtain Δx\Delta xΔx and Δy\Delta yΔy. Their ratio is the slope used to compute the sum. For a nonzero denominator in the prime field, we can write that ratio as multiplication by an inverse:

λ=ΔyΔx=Δy (Δx)−1(modp).\lambda=\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}=\Delta y\,(\Delta x)^{-1}\pmod p.λ=ΔxΔy​=Δy(Δx)−1(modp).

We can find the inverse by reducing the denominator together with the prime. Euclid's algorithm expresses their greatest common divisor as an integer combination of the two inputs. Here that divisor is 1. Reducing the resulting identity modulo the prime removes the prime's contribution and leaves the inverse:

aΔx+bp=1⟹aΔx=1(modp)⟹a=(Δx)−1(modp).a\Delta x+bp=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a\Delta x=1\pmod p\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a=(\Delta x)^{-1}\pmod p.aΔx+bp=1⟹aΔx=1(modp)⟹a=(Δx)−1(modp).

In our example, Euclid gives 3⋅5−2⋅7=13\cdot5-2\cdot7=13⋅5−2⋅7=1. Thus multiplying by 3 undoes multiplication by 5 modulo 7. Applying it to the numerator gives 4⋅3=12≡54\cdot3=12\equiv54⋅3=12≡5. We have now obtained the quotient through a computation on the denominator and the prime.

A quantum circuit could store that inverse and then multiply by it. The paper saves space by keeping the sequence of reductions instead. Binary gcd uses only swaps, subtractions, and halving. Once those decisions have been recorded, the same sequence can act directly on the numerator.

The Dialog construction makes this precise. It records the denominator's reduction, replays the record on a pair containing the numerator and zero, and reverses record construction. The complete operation preserves the denominator, replaces the numerator by the quotient, and returns the working qubits to zero:

∣Δx⟩∣Δy⟩∣0⟩work⟼∣Δx⟩∣Δy(Δx)−1 mod p⟩∣0⟩work.|\Delta x\rangle|\Delta y\rangle|0\rangle_{\rm work}\longmapsto|\Delta x\rangle|\Delta y(\Delta x)^{-1}\bmod p\rangle|0\rangle_{\rm work}.∣Δx⟩∣Δy⟩∣0⟩work​⟼∣Δx⟩∣Δy(Δx)−1modp⟩∣0⟩work​.

For the 256-bit problem, this avoids retaining a separate 256-bit inverse. The record itself occupies space, but the circuit stores it where the shrinking gcd remainders have released qubits. We can now ask how to make each recorded reduction cheaper.

The circuit below shows the three stages: build the record, apply it, and erase it. The full replay lesson follows an example through all three. In this lesson we focus on the arithmetic inside the first stage.

IonQ changes the current numbers, while still saving the decisions

We have just learned to build a gcd record and replay it on the numerator. Building that record still requires intermediate numbers: at each step, inspect the current remainders, decide what to do, update them, and save the decision. The current numbers and the accumulated record therefore coexist.

IonQ changes the representation of those current numbers in the working registers. It still records the decisions. Record and replay comes from the earlier construction; the change here makes the arithmetic used to produce the record cheaper. The circuit below separates these two logical roles. In the compact implementation, shrinking remainders release physical storage for the growing record.

Start from the ordinary gcd update

Keep u odd. If v is even, halve it. If v is odd, first subtract u, after any swap needed to orient the operands, and then halve. With u=3, the even input v=8 becomes 4; the odd input v=5 becomes 1. Let a be the low bit of v. These two cases are

v′=v−au2.v'=\frac{v-au}{2}.v′=2v−au​.

The circuit must choose between subtracting u and doing no subtraction. That controlled arithmetic is the operation IonQ replaces.

Store the even case differently

When v is even, store v+u in its place. When v is odd, store v unchanged. Since u is odd, the stored value is odd in both cases. Call it ṽ; the record still retains the branch information needed to interpret and reverse the computation.

v~=v+(1−a)u.\widetilde v=v+(1-a)u.v=v+(1−a)u.

Take u=3 and v=8. The current register holds 11. The ordinary next value is 4, whose new stored representation is 4+3=7. We obtain that stored result by adding and halving: (11+3)/2=7. For v=5, the current register holds 5. The ordinary next value is 1, already odd, so subtracting and halving gives its stored result: (5−3)/2=1.

The two cases now use addition or subtraction, rather than subtraction or no arithmetic. To select the sign, compute the parity a′ of the next ordinary remainder. Subtracting u from ṽ gives twice that remainder. Both low bits are one, so their subtraction produces no borrow into bit 1; the next parity is simply the XOR of the second-lowest bits:

a′=v′ mod 2=v~[1]⊕u[1].a'=v'\bmod2=\widetilde v[1]\oplus u[1].a′=v′mod2=v[1]⊕u[1].

Re-expressing the next remainder in the same storage convention then gives

v~′=v~+(−1)a′u2.\boxed{\widetilde v'=\frac{\widetilde v+(-1)^{a'}u}{2}.}v′=2v+(−1)a′u​.​
Ordinary inputStored inputParity from bit 1Stored update
(3,8)(3,8)(3,8)(3,11)(3,11)(3,11)1⊕1=01\oplus1=01⊕1=0(11+3)/2=7(11+3)/2=7(11+3)/2=7
(3,5)(3,5)(3,5)(3,5)(3,5)(3,5)1⊕0=11\oplus0=11⊕0=1(5−3)/2=1(5-3)/2=1(5−3)/2=1

After the signed update, we must orient the remainders for the following step. The swap bit is m=a′[u>v~′]m=a'[u>\widetilde v']m=a′[u>v′], where the bracket is 1 when its condition holds. Thus only the odd branch requires a comparison. Keeping this decision in the record lets the inverse circuit undo the swap.

One adder supplies both signs

Why is always adding or subtracting cheaper? The sign can control simple bit flips around one ordinary adder, instead of controlling the carry computation inside it. To see the identity, complement every bit of a width-www target. This changes zzz to J(z)=2w−1−zJ(z)=2^w-1-zJ(z)=2w−1−z. Add uuu, then complement again:

J(J(z)+u)=z−u(mod2w).J(J(z)+u)=z-u\pmod{2^w}.J(J(z)+u)=z−u(mod2w).
A control bit can turn both complements on or off using CNOTs. The carry circuit always performs the same addition; it does not need an extra control at each carry.

The replay must use a matching change of variables. For field registers r,sr,sr,s, the paper stores s~=s−(1−a)r\widetilde s=s-(1-a)rs=s−(1−a)r, giving the partner update s~′=s~−(−1)a′r(modp)\widetilde s'=\widetilde s-(-1)^{a'}r\pmod ps′=s−(−1)a′r(modp). Here rrr denotes a register, not the curve's group order. Recorded swaps and the required modular halves or doubles complete the replay.

The prime-modulus boundary still matters

The integer complement identity needs attention when used in a prime field. For p=2n−cp=2^n-cp=2n−c, complementing gives J(z)≡−z+c−1(modp)J(z)\equiv-z+c-1\pmod pJ(z)≡−z+c−1(modp). The constant cancels around an exact modular adder, but c−1c-1c−1 inputs produce bit strings at least ppp. The circuit must account for those representations, including its approximate 0↔p0\leftrightarrow p0↔p correction when a sum reaches ppp.

Exact identities; finite arithmetic windows

The variable change is exact; the finite circuit saves further work by truncating its arithmetic. Table X uses 1.413n+2.4n1.413n+2.4\sqrt n1.413n+2.4n​ iterations, width n−i/1.413+2.3nn-i/1.413+2.3\sqrt nn−i/1.413+2.3n​ at iteration iii, comparison width 40+2.3n40+2.3\sqrt n40+2.3n​, 37 special-case rounds, 65-bit corrections, and 32-bit phase comparisons. Applying these formulas requires integer rounding and clipping. In a million sampled inputs, each direction had 21 failures, counting wrong values, residual phases, and uncleared workspace. Those observations supply the statistical bound used in the success analysis.

Notation and physical meaning

Definitions are also given where they are used. Open the full notation page.

ppp — field prime
Coordinates lie in the finite field Fp\mathbb F_pFp​, the integers modulo ppp. For secp256k1, p=2256−232−977p=2^{256}-2^{32}-977p=2256−232−977. This modulus controls coordinate arithmetic. Use in the construction
ppp — local error probability
On architecture and state-preparation pages, ppp is the error probability specified beside the formula: for example, a physical two-qubit Pauli error rate or an injected-state fault rate. Each model defines the event and operation counted. Arithmetic pages instead use ppp for the field prime. Use in the construction
rrr — subgroup order
The number of distinct multiples of the generator point PPP; [r]P=O[r]P=\mathcal O[r]P=O. Scalar recovery is modulo rrr, not the field prime ppp. Use in the construction
ddd — secret scalar
The unknown element of Zr\mathbb Z_rZr​ satisfying Q=[d]PQ=[d]PQ=[d]P. Recovering it is the elliptic-curve discrete logarithm problem. Use in the construction
P,Q,OP,Q,\mathcal OP,Q,O — curve points
PPP is the chosen generator, QQQ is the public input point, and O\mathcal OO is the identity element of the curve group. [a]P[a]P[a]P denotes repeated point addition. Use in the construction
ccc — small prime offset
p=2n−cp=2^n-cp=2n−c, so 2n≡c(modp)2^n\equiv c\pmod p2n≡c(modp). For secp256k1, n=256n=256n=256 and c=232+977c=2^{32}+977c=232+977. This relation makes reduction of high bits cheap. Use in the construction
www — scalar-window width
The number of scalar bits handled by one coherent point lookup. The main loop uses w=16w=16w=16, giving tables indexed by 16-bit addresses. Use in the construction
λ\lambdaλ — point-addition slope
For distinct affine points with different x coordinates, λ=(y2−y1)/(x2−x1)\lambda=(y_2-y_1)/(x_2-x_1)λ=(y2​−y1​)/(x2​−x1​) in Fp\mathbb F_pFp​. The division means multiplication by a modular inverse. Elsewhere the same Greek letter may denote a Poisson mean; each lesson specifies its domain. Use in the construction
pfp_fpf​ — approximate-oracle failure bound
For each fixed input pair, an upper bound over fresh random masks on producing either wrong coordinates or a wrong relative phase. Appendix B obtains pf≤0.03346p_f\le0.03346pf​≤0.03346. Use in the construction
P0P_0P0​ — ideal algorithm success
Success probability assigned to exact arithmetic with the selected quantum Fourier measurement and classical recovery procedure. The rigorous and heuristic starting estimates must be kept separate. Use in the construction
QFT / iQFT — quantum Fourier transform
A unitary change of basis between a modular coordinate and its phase frequency. iQFT denotes its inverse. Measuring the result exposes the periodic relation used to recover the secret scalar. Use in the construction
CCX — Toffoli gate
The three-bit reversible map (a,b,t)↦(a,b,t⊕ab)(a,b,t)\mapsto(a,b,t\oplus ab)(a,b,t)↦(a,b,t⊕ab). It is a controlled-controlled-X gate and the main non-Clifford logical resource of the arithmetic. Use in the construction
CCZ — controlled-controlled-Z
The three-qubit unitary ∣a,b,c⟩↦(−1)abc∣a,b,c⟩|a,b,c\rangle\mapsto(-1)^{abc}|a,b,c\rangle∣a,b,c⟩↦(−1)abc∣a,b,c⟩. Conjugating its third qubit by Hadamards gives a Toffoli. A CCZ resource state is CCZ∣+⟩⊗3\mathrm{CCZ}|+\rangle^{\otimes3}CCZ∣+⟩⊗3. Use in the construction
TTT — pi-over-four phase gate
T=diag⁡(1,eiπ/4)T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})T=diag(1,eiπ/4). A T state, up to the convention specified in a lesson, supplies this non-Clifford phase through state injection. The symbol TTT also denotes time in resource equations, where units are explicit. Use in the construction
Clifford frame — tracked logical transformation
A Clifford unitary maps Pauli operators to Pauli operators by conjugation. Instead of applying every such gate physically, the controller can track the accumulated map and reinterpret later measurements. Use in the construction
CliNR — Clifford noise-reduction protocol
Logical CliNR uses a prepared, checked Clifford resource and teleportation. Here it is used to clear a complicated tracked Clifford frame and restore simple logical-measurement representatives. Use in the construction
Q102 — main memory code
The quantum code [[102,22,9]][[102,22,9]][[102,22,9]]: 102 data qubits encode 22 logical qubits with distance 9. Device counts additionally include syndrome ancillas and replacement ions. Use in the construction
Q66 — factory code
The quantum code [[66,4,10]][[66,4,10]][[66,4,10]]: 66 data qubits encode four logical qubits with distance 10. It protects the CCZ-factory state and supports the specific representatives tabulated in Appendix G. Use in the construction
C6 — six-qubit detection code
The [[6,2,2]][[6,2,2]][[6,2,2]] code encodes two logical qubits. In the factory it prepares a pair of low-error logical H states using error detection and postselection. Use in the construction
Cat state — shared parity-measurement resource
A length-m cat is (∣0⟩⊗m+∣1⟩⊗m)/2(|0\rangle^{\otimes m}+|1\rangle^{\otimes m})/\sqrt2(∣0⟩⊗m+∣1⟩⊗m)/2​. Each cat qubit touches at most one target qubit when measuring a product Pauli operator, limiting fault spread. Use in the construction
POC — physical operation cycle
The basic physical timing unit used in the architecture, 0.2 ms0.2\,\mathrm{ms}0.2ms. Gate, transport, and syndrome schedules are expressed in these units. Use in the construction
SEC — syndrome-extraction cycle
One repeated measurement of the code's error checks with its physical schedule. Q102 takes 27 POCs per SEC; Q66 takes 17 POCs per SEC under the stated architecture. Use in the construction
LM / LM2 — logical measurement
LM denotes a measurement of a logical Pauli operator. LM2 spans two code blocks and requires resources that join their local cat states. A logical operation can take several SECs to achieve enough readout confidence. Use in the construction
supp⁡(P)\operatorname{supp}(P)supp(P) — Pauli support
The physical qubits on which a Pauli string PPP acts as X, Y, or Z rather than I. Its cardinality is the operator weight. Commuting operators need not have disjoint supports. Use in the construction
Logical representative — physical realization of an encoded Pauli
Different physical Pauli strings can implement the same logical operation because multiplying by a stabilizer leaves the encoded action unchanged. Choosing representatives controls weight and parallel compatibility. Use in the construction
gcd — greatest common divisor
The largest integer dividing two inputs. Binary-gcd updates use parity tests, subtraction, and division by two. Recording and replaying these updates implements modular multiplication or division reversibly. Use in the construction
κ\kappaκ — truncated carry width
The number of low bits through which a small modular correction is allowed to propagate. A carry beyond that range is one of the approximate arithmetic failure events. Use in the construction
DmeasD_{\rm meas}Dmeas​ — charged measurement depth
The sum of scheduled logical-measurement layers, including the expected penalties used in the resource accounting: 75,251,329 for the reported computation. Use in the construction
τ\tauτ — seconds per charged layer
Appendix E23 uses the unrounded value 0.0294958 s0.0294958\,\mathrm{s}0.0294958s. Table I displays it as 29.50 ms. Runtime is DmeasτD_{\rm meas}\tauDmeas​τ. Use in the construction
Postselection — accept only verified preparations
A preparation attempt is retained only if specified measurement checks pass; otherwise it restarts. Output error is conditioned on acceptance, and retries affect throughput. Use in the construction
pswapp_{\rm swap}pswap​ — survivor-displacement probability
Conditional on a two-qubit interaction involving a loss, the probability that the surviving ion is displaced to the other position. It is not the ordinary two-qubit Pauli error probability. Use in the construction
